{{Short description|Smallest lattice in which the elements of a set are incomparable}}
{{distinguish|text = a lattice on the [[Matroid#Flats|flats of a matroid]], which is sometimes also called a "flat lattice"}}

In [[mathematics]], in the area of [[order theory]], the '''flat lattice''' on a multielement set{{nbsp}}<math>X</math> is the smallest [[Lattice (order)|lattice]] containing the elements of <math>X</math> in which those elements are all pairwise incomparable; equivalently, it is the rank-3 lattice where <math>X</math> is exactly the set of elements of intermediate rank.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Brink|first1=Chris|last2=Kahl|first2=Wolfram|last3=Schmidt|first3=Gunther|date=23 April 1997|title=Relational Methods in Computer Science|location=Vienna, Austria|publisher=Springer Vienna|page=127|isbn=978-3-211-82971-4}}</ref><ref name="order">{{cite conference|last1=Berghammer|first1=Rudolf|last2=von Karger|first2=Burghard|date=12 September 1990|title=Relational Semantics of Functional Programs|book-title=Expert Systems in Engineering: Principles and Applications|conference=the International Workshop on Expert Systems in Engineering|publisher=Springer|page=105|isbn=978-3-540-53104-3}}</ref><ref name="algebraic">{{cite conference|last1=Knoop|first1=Jens|date=August 19, 1998|title=Parallel Constant Propagation|volume=Workshop 4: Automatic Parallelisation and High-Performance Compilers|book-title=Euro-Par'98 Parallel Processing|conference=4th International Euro-Par Conference|location=Southampton, UK|publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg|pages=449–450|isbn=978-3-540-64952-6}}</ref>

==Formal definition==

As a [[partially ordered set]], the flat lattice on a multielement set <math>X</math> is given by<ref name="order" /> <math>(X \cup \{\top, \bot\}, \preceq)</math> where
<math display=block>\forall a, b. a \preceq b \leftrightarrow a = \bot \lor a = b \lor b = \top.</math>

As an algebraic structure, the flat lattice is equivalently given by<ref name="algebraic" /> <math>(X \cup \{\top, \bot\}, \sqcap, \sqcup)</math> where
<math display=block>
\forall a, b. a \sqcap b = \begin{cases}
\bot & \text{if } a = \bot \lor b = \bot\\
\bot & \text{if } a \in X \land b \in X \land a \ne b\\
a    & \text{if } a = b\\
a    & \text{if } b = \top\\
b    & \text{if } a = \top\\
\end{cases}
</math>
and symmetrically for join:
<math display=block>
\forall a, b. a \sqcup b = \begin{cases}
\top & \text{if } a = \top \lor b = \top\\
\top & \text{if } a \in X \land b \in X \land a \ne b\\
a    & \text{if } a = b\\
a    & \text{if } b = \bot\\
b    & \text{if } a = \bot\\
\end{cases}
</math>

All of the cases in the algebraic definition follow from the general lattice axioms except for the <math>a \in X \land b \in X \land a \ne b</math> cases; the poset definition implies them because elements of <math>X</math> are incomparable, so <math>\bot</math> (respectively <math>\top</math>) is the only remaining possibility for the value of the meet (respectively join).

Similarly, the algebraic definition implies the poset definition because no two distinct elements have a nontrivial meet or join, so the only relations that are possible are those that are mandatory from the lattice axioms—exactly the three disjuncts listed.

Finally, the flat lattice on <math>X</math> may be defined implicitly, as the least lattice in which the elements of <math>X</math> are incomparable. This too is equivalent: Consider any lattice on <math>X</math> where the set's elements are pairwise incomparable. Because they are multiple and incomparable, none of them can be the lattice top or bottom, and since <math>X</math> is nonempty, <math>\top</math> and <math>\bot</math> must be distinct. Therefore, <math>X \cup \{\top, \bot\}</math> is the smallest possible set such a lattice could be defined on, and incomparability and the lattice axioms wholly determine the element relations to match the definitions above.

==The flat lattice of an empty set or of a singleton==
The three definitions above, however, do not agree when <math>X</math> is the [[empty set]] or a singleton, as the implicit definition would then collapse lattice elements. Possible resolutions are to exclude these cases (as above), to define the flat lattice of such a set to be the one-element lattice (in agreement with the implicit definition) or to define it as the two- or three-element lattice (in agreement with the explicit constructions).
